         LINK N3 OPPOSITION LANDOWNERS’ REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS TO
                          PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

         Link N3 Opposition Landowners (Link N3 Opponents) file the Replies to Exceptions to

  the Proposal for Decision (PFD). Pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies Memorandum, filed on

  August 20, 2026, these replies are timely filed on or before September 9, 2026.

                                            I.   INTRODUCTION

         On March 26, 2026, Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and LCRA

  Transmission Services Corporation (LCRA) (collectively, the Applicants) filed a joint application

  (Application) with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend their

  certificates of convenience and necessity (CCNs) to construct, own, and operate a proposed Bell

  County East to Big Hill 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line (Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project)

  in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom

  Green, and Williamson counties, Texas. 1



         1
             Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1 (Application) at 5 (Mar. 26, 2026).
                                                                                                     Page 3 of 10


        On August 20, 2026, the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) issued its PFD

in this proceeding.2        The PFD recommended that the Application be denied because the

“Applicants have not established that the amendment of Applicants’ CCNs is necessary for the

service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.” 3                       The PFD additionally

recommended that the Application be denied because the Applicants failed to comply with

16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 22.52(a)(4).4

        The PFD then recommended Route 894, if the Commission determines that the Application

should not be denied.5

        The Link N3 Opponents filed exceptions to the PFD only on its routing recommendation

on September 2, 2026.6 The Link N3 Opponents respond only to the Moseley Group of Intervenors

and the V8 Landowners Coalition (Moseley Group) who filed exceptions to the PFD regarding the

Colorado River Crossing at Link J22 on Route 894 7 and to the Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed (Sneeds)

who filed exceptions in support of Route 891. 8 Additionally, in these replies to exceptions the

Link N3 Opponents also adopt the Save the Lampasas’s replies to exceptions regarding need for

the CCN.

                           II.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF REPLIES

        The Moseley Group’s argument that the Colorado River crossing at Link J22 is superior to

that of Link U3 and the Sneeds’ argument that Route 891 should be selected by the Commission

are not consistent with relevant routing factors. Route 894’s and Route 891’s use of Link J22 is

destructive to the Texas Hill County and Colorado River and the Colorado Bend State Park and

the Post Oak Ridge State Park.

        Route 2969 or Route 296 Option A, which travel through the southern portion of the Study

Area, are superior to Route 894 and Route 891 and protect the devastating impacts to the Colorado

River and Texas State Parks which have continuously been protected as shown through prior

Commission precedent.

                                       III.    APPLICABLE LAW

        The routing selection is governed by Public Utilities Regulatory Act § 37.056(c) and the

Commission’s rules found in 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). As noted by the PFD, in selecting a

route, the Commission “is required to exercise its ‘expertise’ to further the overall public

interest.”10 Additionally, the Commission’s prior precedent has emphasized protecting the Texas

Hill County and minimizing impacts to rivers that run through the area. For instance, the

Commission denied the proposed transmission line in Docket No. 37448 noting the following: 11




        9
         Throughout its rerplies, the N3 Opposition Landowners refer to Route 296 with the modification to Link
F34 to move the link more than 1,000 feet away from Florence Elementary School. Please see Link N3 Opposition
Landowners’ Limited Exceptions to the Alternative Recommendation in Proposal for Decision at fn. 3.
        10
            PFD at 15 (citing Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex. v. Texland Elec. Co., 701 S.W.2d 261, 267 (Tex.App-Austin
1985, writ ref’d n.r.e.).
        11
            Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and
Necessity for the Gillespie to Newton 345-kV CREZ Transmission Line in Gillespie, Llano, San Saba, Burnet, and
Lampasas Counties, Texas, Docket No. 37448, Order at Finding of Facts No. 4 (Apr. 28, 2010).
                                                                                                     Page 5 of 10


        [t]he project was intended to be located in the Texas Hill Country of Central Texas
        spanning Gillespie, Burnet, Llano, and Lampasas Counties. As proposed, the
        transmission line would have traversed portions of rugged terrain through the Hill
        Country, including several river crossings. The land that would have been involved
        is mostly undeveloped ranch land, except for some rural residential developments
        and small towns, but the area is also known for its viewscapes and other scenic
        areas, including Enchanted Rock.

The Commission also recognized the scenic value of the Texas Hill County area in Docket

No. 38354, where it chose a route that ran along I-10 stating that “[i]t is far more likely that a 345-

kV line will be lost in the visual foreground along I-10 than if it were run along a central or northern

route through what is undoubtedly the aesthetically pleasing and relatively undeveloped Texas Hill

Country.”12

        When considering the overall public interest along with prior Commission precedent, the

Commission should not select Route 894 or Route 891. Route 296 and Route 296 Option A better

balance the routing factors as a whole.

                                  IV.     REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS

A.      Routing Criteria

        Link N3 Opponents ask that the Commission focus on two routing factors, recreational and

park areas and prudent avoidance, and stand by their prior briefing and exceptions for the

remaining factors.

        1.       Recreational and Park Areas

        As briefly discussed above, the choice of Route 894 or 891 as advocated by the Moseley

Group and the Sneeds would be devastating to the Colorado River and the Colorado Bend and Post

Oak Ridge State Parks. The PFD notes that the Link J22 Colorado River crossing is outside the


        12
           Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for
the Proposed McCamey D to Kendall to Gillespie 345-KV CREZ Transmission Line in Schleicher, Sutton, Menard,
Kimble, Mason, Gillespie, Kerr, and Kendall Counties, Docket No. 38354, Order at Finding of Fact No. 52 (Jan. 24,
2011).
                                                                                                Page 6 of 10


one-half mile distance of the state parks in the area, 13 and the Mosley Group states in its exceptions

that Link J22 runs perpendicular to the Colorado River rather than parallel. 14 This clearly does not

provide justification for recommending Route 894, when there is substantial testimony on the

determinantal effects of Route 894 on recreational and park areas, especially in terms of Link J22.

Importantly, Texas Parks and Wildlife (TPWD) notes in its viewshed analysis that any 150-200

foot transmission line within 5 miles of a scenic viewpoint is likely to be distracting to visitors and

considered within the foreground visual zone of the viewpoint. 15 Route 894’s Link J22 would pass

within 0.61 miles of the south end of Post Oak Ridge State Park. 16 Even more importantly, Link

J22 would cross the Colorado River just over 4,000 feet from Post Oak Falls, which TPWD

identified as an area of high visitation with multiple scenic overlooks for an iconic waterfall. 17

Furthermore, while the Mosley Group states that Link J22 runs perpendicular to the Colorado

River at its crossing instead of parallel, Links J22-J23-J27 parallel the southern and southwestern

edges of both parks.18 These links are also contained in Route 891 recommended by the Sneeds. 19

       Choosing Route 894 would not be consistent with Commission precedent. Not only has the

Commission ordered routing that minimized impacts to the Texas Hill Country in Docket No.

38354,20 it also did so in Docket No. 38290, where the Commission intentionally chose a route

that was slightly more expensive and crossed more habitable structures than the “best meets” route

because it avoided the scenic Palo Duro Canyon area. 21 In Docket No. 37448, the Commission

denied the application that impacted the area near Colorado Bend State Park. 22

        Lastly, the Environmental Assessment notes that comments from public participation

meetings included comments on aesthetics and parks and recreation areas, including Colorado

Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park. 23 The Commission in Docket No. 45866 rejected

the route chosen in the proposal for decision in favor of a route that avoided Williamson County

Regional Park noting that it would “therefore have a smaller impact on the community’s enjoyment

of local parks.”24

        Clearly, the Commission has maintained that minimizing impacts to Texas’ State Parks

and especially the Texas Hill Country are important and that consideration should be given

sufficient weight in choosing a route in this proceeding. As such, it should not choose Route 894

or 891 due to its impacts on these areas.

        2.        Prudent Avoidance

        The Link N3 Opponents respond to the Sneeds’ argument that simply count the number of

habitable structures within 500 feet of a proposed route as part of the Commission’s routing

analysis. First, focusing on a counting of habitable structures runs counter to the Commission rule

which states that whether a route conforms with the policy of prudent avoidance must be




        21
             Application of Sharyland Utilities, LP to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the
Hereford to White Deer 345-KV CREZ Transmission Line (Formerly Panhandle AB to Panhandle BA) in Armstrong,
Cason, Deaf Smith, Oldham, Potter, and Randall Counties, Docket No. 38290, Order at Finding of Fact No. 33 (Dec.
13, 2010); see also Docket No. 38290, PFD at 10 (Nov. 9, 2010) for number of habitable structures within 500-feet of
route centerline.
        22
             Docket No. 37448, Order at 1 and Finding of Fact Nos. 34, 41.
        23
             Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1 at 84, 172-73.
        24
             Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend a Certificate of Convenience and
Necessity for the Round Rock-Leander 138-kV Transmission Line in Williamson County, Docket No. 45866, Order at
1-2 (Jun. 6, 2017).
                                                                                                        Page 8 of 10


considered as part of the routing analysis.25 This is not equivalent to a mere counting of habitable

structures.26

        This is why in numerous Competitive Renewable Energy Zone (CREZ) transmission line

cases, the most analogous transmission line cases to the applications that face the Commission

today, the Commission repeatedly set the precedent that the Commissioners do not solely count

the number of habitable structures on a route to determine prudent avoidance.                          In Docket

No. 37464, the Commission chose a route that impacted an additional 22 habitable structures

because, when analyzed holistically, it did a better job of supporting community values and

protecting environmental integrity and natural aesthetics by crossing the Lampasas River at a

previously disturbed site, rather than crossing the river at a pristine location. 27 In Docket No.

38230, the Commission chose a route that did not affect the least amount of habitable structures in

part because it ranked the best on impact to wooded areas, wetland forest, streams, and length

parallel to existing corridors and property boundaries. 28 In Docket No. 38354, the Commission

balanced the competing factors of avoiding the Hill Country and avoiding habitable structures by

choosing a route that performed well on both issues, rather than the best on either. 29 And in Docket

No. 37448, the Commission did not grant an application in part because of its effect on the exact

same Texas State Park that would be scarred by Routes 894 and 891.30 With the benefit of

hindsight, we can see that the Commission’s decisions in these CREZ cases threaded the needle

and lead to generally satisfied stakeholders who do not hold grudges today after participating in

proceedings that could have been particularly thorny and contentious if the Commissioners had

not followed the Legislature’s well-reasoned set of routing criteria that have stood the test of time.

         The Staten Creek Intervenors in their exceptions, correctly note that Route 296, a southern

routing option, mitigates the destructive impacts of Route 894 to Texas’ State Parks. 31 As noted

by the Link N3 Opponents and Save the Lampasas in their exceptions, Route 296’s impact on the

Florence elementary school and the two neighboring churches can be entirely resolved by either

using mitigating engineering, or even better, by slightly altering the route to completely avoid the

school and churches.32 Given that consideration, along with correctly applying the Commission’s

standard of prudent avoidance, the Commission should reject utilizing Route 894 or 891, routes

whose impacts on the beauty and aesthetics of the Texas Hill Country, cannot be mitigated or

undone.

         Overall, the Link N3 Opponents support the PFD’s denial of the application on the basis

of need. However, in the absence of denial of the Application, the Commission should not choose

Route 894 or Route 891as it would devastate the Texas Hill Country in disregard of Commission

precedent. Instead, Route 296 and 296 Option A should be chosen as it best considers the overall

public interest in protecting these critical natural resources of the State.




         31
              Staten Creek Ranch’s Exceptions to the PFD at 39 (Sept. 2, 2026).
         32

Save the Lampasas’ Exceptions to the Alternative Recommendation in the PFD (Sept. 2, 2026).

                                       V.   CONCLUSION

       For these reasons, Link N3 Opponents respectfully request that the Commission approve

Route 296 or 296 Option A. Link N3 Opponents respectfully request any other relief to which it

has shown itself justly entitled.
